question:
A unit hexagram is composed of a regular hexagon of side length \(1\) and its \(6\) equilateral triangular extensions, as shown in the diagram. What is the ratio of the area of the extensions to the area of the original hexagon?

[Figure 1](figures/2007_AMC_8_Q12_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The regular hexagon can be divided into triangles that match its extensions. Join its center to all six vertices. Regularity gives equal center-to-vertex lengths and six equal central angles, each measuring
\[
\frac{360^\circ}{6}=60^\circ.
\]
Each resulting triangle is isosceles with a \(60^\circ\) vertex angle, so its other two angles are also \(60^\circ\). Thus it is equilateral, with side length \(1\), just like each extension.

These six triangles fill the hexagon without overlapping interiors. Let \(t>0\) be the area of one equilateral triangle of side length \(1\). The extensions have total area \(6t\), and the original hexagon also has area \(6t\). Hence the requested ratio is
\[
6t:6t=1:1,
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\mathrm{A}}\).
